entry: Role-playing video game for the [[PlayStation]], seventh main installment of the [[Final Fantasy]] series. Developed and published by Square and released in 1997, it follows the mercenary Cloud Strife, who joins an eco-terrorist group opposing a megacorporation that uses the planet's life essence as energy. It was the first in the series to use full motion video and 3D computer graphics, and it received widespread critical acclaim. It sold more than 9.9 million copies on PlayStation alone.

Nazi plan for the total extermination of the Jews during World War II. The name was a [[Euphemism|euphemism]] for murder. The plan likely began in 1941 and was formally revealed to non-SS German leaders at the Wannsee Conference in January 1942. It culminated in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], in which approximately 6 million Jews were murdered.

Illegal activity involving money, finance or financial systems, committed for personal or organizational gain. It includes crimes against [[Property|property]], involving the unlawful conversion of ownership to one's own use. [[Fraud]] takes many forms, including check, credit card, mortgage, insurance and securities fraud, insider trading and market manipulation. Other offenses include scams, tax evasion, [[Corruption|corruption]] (including bribery, embezzlement and extortion), [[Identity theft]], money laundering and forgery. Such crimes may be committed by individuals, corporations or [[Organized crime|organized crime]] groups, and may also involve computer crime, elder abuse and violent crimes such as [[Robbery|robbery]] or [[Murder|murder]]. The U.K. Home Office estimated the cost of fraud against individuals and businesses in 2023–2024 at in excess of £14 billion.

Small to medium-sized [[Passerine|passerine]] birds of the family Fringillidae, with stout conical bills adapted for eating seeds and nuts. Finches often have colorful plumage and are usually resident rather than migratory. They have a worldwide native distribution except for [[Australia]] and the polar regions. The family contains more than 200 species divided into 50 [[Genus|genera]], including canaries, siskins, redpolls, grosbeaks, euphonias and the Hawaiian honeycreepers. Other groups also called finches include the estrildid finches of the Old World tropics and Australia, and Darwin's finches of the Galapagos Islands. Finches and canaries were used in coal mines in the U.K., U.S. and Canada to detect [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] from the 18th to the 20th century, a practice that ceased in the U.K. in 1986.

Photography created in line with the photographer's vision as an artist, using the medium for creative expression. Its goal is to express an idea, message or emotion, in contrast to [[Photojournalism|photojournalism]], which documents specific subjects and events, and to commercial photography, which advertises products or services. One historian called John Edwin Mayall the earliest exponent of the form, citing daguerreotypes he exhibited illustrating the Lord's Prayer in 1851. Victorian-era practitioners such as Julia Margaret Cameron, Charles Lutwidge Dodgson and Oscar Gustave Rejlander helped establish it as a fine art. The [[Museum of Modern Art|Museum of Modern Art]] (MoMA) set up a department of photography in 1940, a step often cited as institutional confirmation of its status as an art. Staged, carefully lit pictures by Gregory Crewdson and Jeff Wall are noted for their quality.

Dimensionless physical constant quantifying the strength of the electromagnetic interaction between elementary charged particles. Denoted α, it has a value of approximately 0.0072973525643, or about 1/137.035999177. Arnold Sommerfeld introduced it in 1916 while extending the [[Bohr model]] of the atom to explain the fine structure of the spectral lines of hydrogen. Why it has this value is not understood, and [[Richard Feynman|Richard Feynman]] described it as "one of the greatest damn mysteries of physics."

Multi-jointed digit on the forelimb of [[Tetrapod|tetrapod]] vertebrates with hands, such as humans and other [[Primate|primates]]. It is typically covered by a keratinized nail that protects the fingertip. Most tetrapods have five digits; digits that are notably elongated are called fingers, while shorter ones are called toes. In humans, fingers are opposable, with two or three phalanges each, and serve as an important organ of tactile sensation and fine movement. Human hands contain 14 digital bones, two in the thumb and three in each finger, and each finger has three joints. The muscles that move the finger joints lie in the palm and forearm rather than in the fingers, and flexion is by far the strongest movement.

Sexual stimulation of the vulva, clitoris or vagina using the fingers. It may also stimulate the anus. When one person performs it on another, it is a form of manual sex, analogous to a [[Handjob|handjob]]. It may be used for arousal or [[Foreplay|foreplay]], make up an entire sexual encounter, or be non-penetrative. Massage of the [[Clitoris|clitoris]] is the most common way for a woman to achieve orgasm, and studies indicate that 70–80 percent of women require direct clitoral stimulation to reach orgasm. Fingering the vagina is often performed to stimulate the [[G-spot]]. Fingering one's own vulva or vagina is a form of [[Masturbation|masturbation]].

Impression left by the friction ridges of a human finger, used as a biometric identifier. Human fingerprints are detailed, unique, difficult to alter and durable over a lifetime, making them suitable as long-term markers of identity. Partial prints recovered from crime scenes are an important method of [[Forensic science|forensic science]]. Fingerprint matching is among the most widely used and most reliable biometric techniques. Friction ridge patterns form around the 15th week of fetal development and remain until after death. The patterns are hereditary, and monozygotic [[Twin|twins]] have very similar, though not identical, fingerprints. Academics have argued that the error rate in fingerprint matching has not been adequately studied, and that fingerprint evidence lacks a secure statistical foundation.

Mathematical model of computation, an abstract machine that is in exactly one of a finite number of states at any given time. It moves from one state to another in response to inputs, and each change is called a transition. A finite-state machine has less computational power than a [[Turing machine]], because its memory is limited by its number of states. Such machines underlie regular expressions and model everyday devices such as vending machines, elevators and traffic lights.

Nordic country in Northern Europe, officially the Republic of Finland (pop., 2026: 5,662,086). Its capital and largest city is [[Helsinki]], and its official languages are Finnish and Swedish. Boreal forest covers much of the land, and there are more than 180,000 lakes. Part of Sweden from the 13th century, Finland was captured in 1809 and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire. It declared independence after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and in World War II it fought the [[Soviet Union]] in the [[Winter War]] and the Continuation War, losing territory but keeping its independence and democracy. Finland joined the [[European Union]] in 1995 and [[NATO]] in 2023. It was the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage, in 1906. After rapid industrialization from the 1950s, it developed an advanced economy and a Nordic-style welfare state.

Experimental novel by the Irish writer [[James Joyce]], published in 1939. Written in English altered with words from many languages, it follows the Earwicker family through a cyclical dream narrative set during a single night in a mythical [[Dublin]]. The novel ends with an unfinished line that completes the fragment with which it began. Its initial reception was largely negative, and it has a reputation as one of the most difficult works in literature.

Islamic jurisprudence, the human understanding and practice of [[Sharia|sharia]]. Muslims regard sharia as immutable and infallible, whereas fiqh is considered fallible and changeable. Fiqh expands and develops sharia through *ijtihad* (independent interpretation) of the [[Quran|Quran]] and the *sunnah*, and jurists issue rulings (*fatwa*) on questions put to them. It deals with ritual observance, morals and social legislation, as well as economic and political systems. Four prominent schools (*madhhabs*) exist within Sunni practice: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. Shi'a practice has two or three. Its study is traditionally divided into *usul al-fiqh*, the principles and methods of legal interpretation, and *furu al-fiqh*, the elaboration of rulings based on those principles.

[[Conifer|Coniferous]] tree of the [[Genus|genus]] *Abies* in the family Pinaceae. Firs often grow 40–60 m tall, with a single straight trunk and a conical crown. Their needle-like evergreen leaves are attached singly to the branches on a circular base, which distinguishes them from other members of the pine family. Unlike [[Spruce|spruces]], firs have erect, cylindrical female cones 5–25 cm long that disintegrate at maturity, releasing winged seeds. Firs occur on mountains across much of North and Central America, Eurasia and North Africa. Their wood is used for pulp, plywood and indoor construction, and some species are grown as Christmas trees. Taxonomists disagree on the number of species, with estimates ranging from 46 to 67.

Any of several stinging ant species of the [[Genus|genus]] *Solenopsis*, which includes more than 200 species. The name is also applied loosely to other ants, including weaver ants of the genus *Oecophylla* in Southeast Asia. The red imported fire ant (*Solenopsis invicta*), native to subtropical South America, was introduced accidentally to the southeastern [[United States|U.S.]] in the 1930s and has spread widely, displacing native ants. Colonies can exceed 250,000 workers and build conspicuous earthen mounds up to 40 cm high. Fire ants bite to get a grip and then sting, injecting an [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] venom that causes burning pain. Stings can cause severe allergic reactions in sensitive people. Management relies on chemical baits and biological controls.

Profession of controlling and extinguishing [[Fire|fires]]; a person who does this is a firefighter. Firefighters undergo technical training in structural and [[Wildfire|wildland]] firefighting, and the work is dangerous because of smoke, oxygen deficiency, high temperatures, poisonous atmospheres and violent air flows. Firefighters carry self-contained breathing apparatus, and operations begin with reconnaissance to locate the fire and identify its risks. Fires are extinguished by removing water, fuel or oxidant, or by chemical flame inhibition, and the extinguisher must suit the fire type, such as grease, paper or electrical. Rome's Vigiles, a force of 7,000 people equipped with buckets and axes who also served as police, were the first organized firefighting force. In the 3rd century BC, the Alexandrian Greek Ctesibius built a double force pump.

Soft-bodied [[Beetle|beetle]] of the family *Lampyridae*, many of whose species produce light. Fireflies are also called lightning bugs or glowworms, and they glow mainly at twilight to attract mates. Light production is thought to have originated as a warning signal to predators, because the larvae were distasteful, and was later co-opted as a mating signal. Females of the genus *Photuris* mimic the flash pattern of *Photinus* males to lure and eat them. Most larvae are predators that feed on other larvae, [[Snail|snails]] and slugs, and most fireflies hibernate as larvae. Adults live a few weeks in summer. Populations are declining in many areas because of habitat loss, artificial light, [[Pesticide|pesticides]] and climate change.

Free, open-source web browser developed by the Mozilla Foundation and its subsidiary, the Mozilla Corporation. It was created in 2002 under the codename "Phoenix" by members of the Mozilla community who wanted a standalone browser. Released on November 9, 2004, it challenged the dominance of [[Internet Explorer]] with 60 million downloads within nine months. It uses the Gecko rendering engine, except on iOS. Its usage share peaked at 32.21% in November 2009 and then declined in competition with [[Google Chrome|Chrome]].

Structure of brick, stone or metal designed to contain a fire and heat a room or dwelling. Historically, fireplaces were also used for cooking and for heating water for laundry and domestic use. A fire is contained in a firebox or fire pit, and a [[Chimney|chimney]] or other flue lets exhaust gas escape. Fireplaces may be fueled by wood, [[Charcoal|charcoal]], [[Coal]], coke, smokeless fuel, [[Propane]], butane, [[Methane]] or ethanol. Manufactured fireplaces have sheet-metal or glass fireboxes, and electric fireplaces may be built in or fitted as inserts. Ventless models release moisture into the room air and need an oxygen sensor and a [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] detector. [[Benjamin Franklin|Benjamin Franklin's]] 1741 Pennsylvania fireplace introduced convective air flow to improve heat distribution. The Environmental Protection Agency warns that "Smoke may smell good, but it's not good for you."

Low-explosive pyrotechnic devices used for aesthetic and entertainment purposes. Fireworks produce four primary effects: noise, light, smoke and floating materials such as confetti. They are classed as ground or aerial. Aerial fireworks may be propelled by a rocket, as skyrockets are, or shot into the air as aerial shells from a [[Mortar (weapon)|mortar]]. Most consist of a paper or pasteboard tube filled with combustible material, often pyrotechnic stars, and several tubes may be combined into shapes. The earliest fireworks came from China during the [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279). Metal salts provide the colors: strontium gives crimson, barium gives green, copper gives blue and sodium gives yellow. Mismanagement can lead to accidents, and China remains the largest manufacturer and exporter of fireworks.

Medieval state in Southeastern Europe, existing from 680–681 to 1018. Founded after Bulgars led by Asparuh settled south of the [[Danube]], the empire came to rule Bulgars and [[Slavs|Slavic]] peoples, who gradually mixed and adopted the Slavic language. Under Simeon I, who was recognized with the title tsar, the empire reached its greatest territorial extent in the late 9th and early 10th centuries and rivaled the [[Byzantine Empire]]. Bulgaria adopted Christianity in 864 and became the cultural and spiritual center of Slavic Europe, where Old Church Slavonic literature spread widely. After a crushing defeat by [[Basil II]] at Kleidion in 1014, the last strongholds surrendered in 1018. The state was succeeded by the [[Second Bulgarian Empire]] in 1185.

Conflict (1994–1996) between the Russian Federation and the separatist Chechen Republic of Ichkeria. Chechnya had come under a secessionist regime led by Dzhokhar Dudayev after the dissolution of the [[Soviet Union]] in 1991. [[Boris Yeltsin]] ordered a military operation in 1994 to "establish constitutional order in Chechnya." Grozny was captured in March 1995, but guerrilla resistance continued, and Dudayev was killed in April 1996. Estimates of Chechen civilian deaths range from 30,000 to 100,000. A peace treaty ended the fighting, but Russia invaded again in 1999, starting the [[Second Chechen War]].

Council of Christian bishops convened by the [[Roman emperor]] Constantine I in Nicaea (now İznik, Turkey) in 325. It met from May to July and was attended by at least 200 bishops, almost all from the eastern half of the [[Roman Empire]]. Also known as the First Ecumenical Council, it was called to resolve a dispute in Alexandria between Archbishop Alexander and the presbyter [[Arius|Arius]] over the nature of Jesus and his relation to God the Father. It produced the first part of the [[Nicene Creed]] and mandated uniform observance of the date of Easter.

Military expedition of 1096–1099 by Western European armies, the first of the [[Crusades|Crusades]] to the Holy Land. [[Pope Urban II]] supported a Byzantine request for help against the Seljuk Turks at the Council of Clermont in 1095 and urged an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Forces led by princes such as Godfrey of Bouillon and Raymond IV of Toulouse marched through Anatolia and captured [[Antioch]] in June 1098. [[Jerusalem]] was stormed on July 15, 1099, and a large fraction of its residents were massacred. Four Crusader states were established, including the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]].

Empire ruled by [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]], from May 18, 1804, to April 6, 1814, and again briefly in 1815. At its height in 1812 it had 130 departments, over 44 million people and about 90 million subjects across Europe. The [[Napoleonic Code]] spread through conquered territories. The 1812 invasion of Russia nearly destroyed the French army, and the empire collapsed in 1814. Napoleon was defeated at the [[Battle of Waterloo|Battle of Waterloo]] in 1815 and exiled to [[Saint Helena]].
